title: How to put a 12-year-old ERP in order before touching it
excerpt: A representative scenario: how a coupled ERP with no documentation is diagnosed, which services are involved and how the change is prioritized.

children.text: This article describes a representative scenario that illustrates how we approach this type of problem. It does not describe work with a specific client, and the results it mentions are expected, not achieved.
The starting point

A mid-sized manufacturer ran a 12-year-old ERP. Its modules were coupled, it had almost no documentation, and every deployment took three weeks to coordinate with the business. Each small change required reviewing much of the system, and the knowledge sat with a few people.
First, understand before changing

The first step was not to rewrite anything. An architecture assessment mapped the dependencies, identified the riskiest modules and separated what the business uses from what was simply there. The method is described in the
architecture assessment
Module boundaries before replacements

Instead of a full replacement, clear boundaries were defined between modules: which data each area owns and which interfaces the others may use. Each change then touched only its boundary, and the modernization could move forward in parts.
The resulting roadmap ordered the modernization in phases, with criteria to move forward. That work is described in the
modernization roadmap
Designing the target architecture

For the priority modules, the solution architecture was designed: components, data flows and integrations with the rest of the system. Every decision was documented with its reason, so the internal team could sustain it without depending on the people who made it. The detail is in the
solution architecture design
Risk governance during the transition
A technical risk register with assigned owners.
Periodic review of architecture decisions.
A simple report for leadership in each phase.
The transition therefore does not depend on a single project: the risk is visible and managed continuously.
What to expect from this approach
The expected results of work like this are lower deployment risk, clear module boundaries and better operational visibility. They are expectations based on the method, not figures from a real case.
How to apply it to your system
If your system has a similar problem, the first step is the same: an assessment that separates the diagnosis from the decision. The full scenario is in our
case studies
